Field studies conducted in the terra firme forests of southeastern Amazonia have provided valuable life-history data for the Black-spotted bare-eye (Phlegopsis nigromaculata), a secretive understory antbird. Incubation experiments, carried out at a constant temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], indicate that the incubation period, and thus the age at hatching, spans approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days]. This duration is comparable to that observed in other medium-sized thamnophilids and aligns with estimates from the congener Akletos goeldii. Newly hatched nestlings emerge with a wet weight of about 5.8 grams [Wwb = about 5.8 grams], a modest mass that reflects the altricial condition typical of suboscine passerines. This initial mass is roughly one-eighth of the adult female body mass, highlighting the substantial parental investment required during the nestling phase. The embryonic development rate, inferred from these incubation parameters, appears to be finely tuned to the stable thermal environment of the nest cavity in lowland tropical forests.

During the nestling phase, Black-spotted bare-eye chicks undergo a rapid transformation from helpless hatchlings to independent juveniles. Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of the breeding season, which average 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones is observed. Fledging, defined as the age at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and departs the nest, occurs at 14.5 days after hatching [tx = 14.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period is characteristic of many antbirds and is thought to be an adaptation that minimizes the risk of nest predation. The chicks are brooded almost continuously for the first several days before they develop sufficient feathering and endothermy. Daily mass gains during this period are substantial, with nestlings often doubling their hatch weight within the first week.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult females of Phlegopsis nigromaculata has been recorded at 45.4 grams [Wwi = 45.4 grams], a value consistent with the sexual size dimorphism observed in many thamnophilids, where females are often slightly larger than males. This body mass represents a significant increase from the 5.8 grams at hatching, a more than sevenfold increase achieved over the course of development. The energetic costs associated with reaching this adult mass are considerable, particularly for growing juveniles navigating the challenges of the forest understory. Field measurements indicate that females reach this asymptotic mass after completing their growth phase, typically around the time of sexual maturation. A comparative analysis with congeneric species suggests that this body size is near the median for the genus Phlegopsis.

The process of sexual maturation in this species is marked by a distinct delay relative to fledging. Puberty, defined as the age at which an individual becomes capable of gamete production, occurs at 43.5 days after hatching [tp = 43.5 days after hatching] under ambient thermal conditions averaging 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This interval allows for the completion of skeletal growth and the acquisition of adult plumage before reproductive effort begins. The age at first successful breeding, however, is considerably deferred, typically not occurring until approximately 1.5 years after hatching [tR = approximately 1.5 years after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay between physiological puberty and actual reproductive activity is common among tropical passerines and may be linked to the time required to establish a breeding territory and find a mate.

Respirometry trials conducted on captive individuals under controlled thermal conditions have quantified the basal metabolic requirements of this species. At a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate was measured at 87.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 87.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate is consistent with the allometric scaling relationships established for suboscine passerines of similar body mass. In terms of population dynamics, the maximum reproductive rate is relatively low, with females laying a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and producing up to two clutches annually [F_R_i = up to two clutches annually]. This modest output, combined with the developmental delays described above, results in a relatively slow life-history pace. Maximum lifespan in the wild is estimated at approximately 9.8 years [am = approximately 9.8 years], a longevity that is typical for a bird of this size in a stable tropic at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]al environment.
